questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve  $r(t)=\sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k$ at the point $P(2,4,8),$  valid for all real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

where ${t}_{0}$ corresponds to the value of $t$ at the point $P.$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k \\ \sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+t}=2 \\ {t}^{2}-5=4 \\ 3t-1=8\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the third equation, we get $t=3.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(3).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1+t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-5)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+t}}\,i+2t\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+(3)}}\,i+2(3)\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}\,i+2\cdot 3\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(2,4,8)$ is

$$
R(u)=2i+4\,j+8\,k+u(\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t}\,,\,\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨0\,,\,1⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{t}\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}\,,\,\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨0\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨0\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨0\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨{e}^{t}\,,\,\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟩ & =0 \\ 0\cdot {e}^{t}+1\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{0}\,,\,\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}}⟩=⟨1\,,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,1).$

evidence.solution_quote: we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,1).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨1-4{t}^{2},5t+1⟩$ at the point where $t=-1,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=-1,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(-1)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(-1)+u{r}^{′}(-1),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨1-4(-1)^{2},5(-1)+1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-8t,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(-1) & =⟨-8(-1),5⟩ \\  & =⟨8,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=-1$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-3,-4⟩+u⟨8,5⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t,3{t}^{2}+9t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,3⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+9t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =⟨c,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3t+4=c \\ 6t+9=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=3t+4.$ Substituting $c=3t+4$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+9 & =3(3t+4) \\ 6t+9 & =9t+12 \\ 3t & =-3 \\ t & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(-1)^{2}+4(-1),3(-1)^{2}+9(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{5}{2},-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-\frac{5}{2},-6).$

evidence.solution_quote: we conclude that $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-\frac{5}{2},-6).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ \frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j & =c(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}i+2t\,j) \\ \frac{1}{t}\,i+({t}^{2}-3)\,j & =-\frac{c}{{t}^{2}}i+2ct\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{t}=-\frac{c}{{t}^{2}} \\ {t}^{2}-3=2ct\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $-t=c.$ Substituting $c=-t$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-3 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 3{t}^{2}-3 & =0 \\ 3(t+1)(t-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =\frac{1}{1}\,i+({1}^{2}-3)\,j \\  & =\,i-2\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,-2).$
